title: APIs
blurb: How software talks to software — HTTP, REST, and building your own.

lessons.title: Consuming an API
lessons.explain: To use an API you send an HTTP request to an endpoint and parse the JSON response. Auth is often a token in a header.
lessons.example:
import requests
r = requests.get('https://api.example.com/users/5',
    headers={'Authorization': 'Bearer TOKEN'})
data = r.json()

lessons.title: REST fundamentals
objectives: Explain what REST means and its core principles
Explain how REST changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect REST with resource and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: REST (Representational State Transfer) is a style for designing web APIs around resources, identified by URLs, manipulated using standard HTTP methods. A REST API is typically stateless -- each request contains everything needed to process it, with no server-side session memory between requests.
examples:
GET /users/42        # get user 42
POST /users          # create a new user
PUT /users/42        # update user 42 entirely
DELETE /users/42     # delete user 42
commonMistakes: Designing an API where the server must remember previous requests to process a new one -- this breaks REST's stateless principle and complicates scaling.
lessons.careerRelevance: REST is the dominant style for web APIs -- fluency here is assumed in almost any backend role.

lessons.title: HTTP methods
objectives: Use GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, and DELETE correctly
Explain how GET changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example

lessons.explanation: GET retrieves data without changing anything (safe to repeat). POST creates a new resource.
examples:
GET /orders/5       # read only, safe to repeat
PATCH /orders/5      # update just one field, e.g. status
DELETE /orders/5     # remove it
commonMistakes: Using GET for an operation that changes data (like deleting something) -- GET requests can be cached, prefetched, or retried automatically, causing unintended side effects.
lessons.careerRelevance: Correct HTTP method usage is a baseline expectation in any REST API design or review.

lessons.title: Status codes
objectives: Interpret common HTTP status codes
Explain how status code changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect status code with 200 and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: HTTP status codes tell a client what happened to a request. Codes in the 2xx range usually mean success, 4xx codes describe client-side problems such as invalid input or missing resources, and 5xx codes indicate server-side failures. Choose a status code that matches the real outcome so callers can handle the response correctly.
examples:
200 OK              -- success
201 Created          -- POST succeeded, new resource made
400 Bad Request      -- client sent invalid data
401 Unauthorized     -- missing/invalid authentication
404 Not Found        -- resource doesn't exist
500 Internal Server Error -- server-side failure
commonMistakes: Returning 200 OK for a request that actually failed -- this misleads clients into thinking something succeeded when it didn't.
lessons.careerRelevance: Correct status codes are essential for clients (and monitoring systems) to know how to react to a response.

objectives: Explain common API authentication approaches
Explain how authentication changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example

lessons.explanation: Authentication proves WHO is making a request. An API key is a simple secret token sent with each request.
examples:
# API key in a header:
GET /data
Authorization: Bearer sk_live_abc123

# vs OAuth: a multi-step flow where the user grants a third-party app
# limited access without ever sharing their actual password with it
commonMistakes: Sending an API key or token in a URL query parameter -- URLs are often logged in plaintext by servers and proxies, exposing the secret.
lessons.careerRelevance: Correct authentication is a core security responsibility of any real API.

lessons.title: Working with JSON
objectives: Read and produce JSON, the standard API data format
Explain how JSON changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect JSON with serialize and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is the standard format most REST APIs use to send and receive structured data -- objects with key-value pairs, arrays, strings, numbers, booleans, and null. Almost every language has built-in or standard-library support to parse JSON into native objects and serialize objects back into JSON.
commonMistakes: Forgetting to set the Content-Type header to application/json when sending a JSON body -- some servers won't parse the body correctly without it.
lessons.careerRelevance: JSON fluency is assumed baseline knowledge for working with virtually any modern web API.

lessons.title: Pagination
objectives: Explain why and how APIs paginate large result sets
Explain how pagination changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect pagination with offset-based and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Returning millions of rows in one response would be slow and memory-heavy for both server and client.
examples:
GET /orders?page=2&limit=20     # offset-based: skip 20, return next 20
GET /orders?cursor=abc123&limit=20  # cursor-based: continue from a specific point
commonMistakes: Returning an entire unbounded dataset in one response with no pagination -- this becomes slow, memory-heavy, and fragile as the dataset grows.
lessons.careerRelevance: Pagination design is a common, practical real API design decision with real performance consequences.

lessons.title: Error handling in APIs
objectives: Design clear, consistent API error responses
Apply the KHDA-benchmarked professional additions in a realistic company workflow: idempotency keys, retry with exponential backoff.
Explain how error handling changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect error handling with error response and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A good API error response includes a meaningful status code AND a structured body explaining what went wrong -- not just a bare error code with no context. Consistent error formats across all endpoints make a client's error-handling code simpler and more reliable.
commonMistakes: Returning inconsistent error formats across different endpoints -- this forces client code to handle each endpoint's errors differently, a real maintenance burden.
lessons.careerRelevance: Clear, consistent error design is a mark of a genuinely well-designed, production-quality API. These additions were retained because they map to practical software/AI work rather than theory-only study.

lessons.title: Rate limiting
objectives: Explain why APIs rate-limit requests and how clients should respond
Explain how rate limiting changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect rate limiting with 429 and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Rate limiting caps how many requests a client can make in a given time window, protecting the server from being overwhelmed (by mistake or by abuse). When the limit is hit, the API typically returns a 429 Too Many Requests status.
examples:
HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests
Retry-After: 30

# a well-behaved client waits at least 30 seconds before retrying,
# and increases the wait further if still rate-limited
commonMistakes: Retrying a rate-limited request immediately in a tight loop -- this makes the underlying problem worse and can extend how long you're limited for.
lessons.careerRelevance: Rate limiting and respecting it correctly is essential for any real client integrating with a third-party API.

lessons.title: API Versioning and Backward Compatibility
objectives: Distinguish backward-compatible changes from breaking changes, and choose a versioning strategy that protects existing clients
Apply the KHDA-benchmarked professional additions in a realistic company workflow: OpenAPI schema contracts, webhooks.
Explain how API versioning changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect API versioning with backward-compatible change and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Once an API has real clients, changing it is no longer just an internal decision -- a breaking change (renaming or removing a field, changing a field's type, changing what a status code means) can crash every client that depends on the old shape, often with no warning.
examples:
# BREAKING: renaming an existing field silently
# /v1/users/42  ->  {"user_name": "asha"}
# becomes
# /v1/users/42  ->  {"username": "asha"}   # same version, field renamed
# any client reading response['user_name'] now crashes or gets undefined -- no warning, no migration window

# CORRECT: introduce the change in a new version instead
# /v1/users/42  ->  {"user_name": "asha"}     # unchanged, old clients keep working
# /v2/users/42  ->  {"username": "asha"}      # new clients opt in when ready
# /v1/ is deprecated with a stated end-of-life date, giving clients time to migrate
commonMistakes: Treating a field rename or type change as a 'small' update that doesn't need a new version -- from a client's perspective, a renamed field is indistinguishable from a removed one, and.
lessons.careerRelevance: Versioning discipline is exactly what separates an API you can safely evolve for years from one that breaks every integration the moment it needs to change -- a routine, expected skill in any real API-facing role. These additions were retained because they map to practical software/AI work rather than theory-only study.

description: How software talks to software — HTTP, REST, and building your own.

interviewPreparation.q: How would you version an API to avoid breaking existing clients?
interviewPreparation.a: Either a URL-based version (/v1/, /v2/) or a version header, with old versions kept running until clients have time to migrate. The key discipline is never changing an existing version's contract in a breaking way -- new fields can usually be added safely, but renaming, removing, or changing the type of an existing field can't happen without a new version.

interviewPreparation.q: Why shouldn't an API return HTTP 200 for a failed request?
interviewPreparation.a: Clients, caches, monitoring, and retry logic all rely on the status code to know whether a request succeeded, not just the response body. Returning 200 for a failed login (for example) means anything downstream that checks status codes -- not just your one hand-written client -- silently treats a failure as a success.

interviewPreparation.q: How do you decide on a pagination strategy for an endpoint returning a large list?
interviewPreparation.a: Offset-based pagination (page/limit) is simple but can skip or repeat items if the underlying data changes between requests; cursor-based pagination is more complex to implement but stays correct under concurrent writes. For a feed that changes frequently, cursor-based is usually worth the extra complexity; for a mostly-static list, offset-based is often fine.

interviewPreparation.q: What would you consider when designing rate limiting for a public API?
interviewPreparation.a: What the limit actually protects against (abuse vs. genuine capacity), what a client sees when they hit it (a clear 429 with a Retry-After header, not a vague error), and whether different endpoints or client tiers need different limits -- a search endpoint and a webhook endpoint have very different real costs.

interviewPreparation.q: What makes API documentation actually useful to someone integrating against it, versus documentation that exists but isn't used?
interviewPreparation.a: Concrete request/response examples for every endpoint, not just a schema; clear documentation of error cases, not just the happy path; and staying accurate as the API changes, since documentation that lies is often worse than no documentation, because it costs someone real debugging time to discover it's wrong.

careerApplications: What most backend internship tickets actually involve building.

capstone.title: Evolve a working API into a stable, versioned public contract
capstone.description: Take a backend service (your Backend course capstone, or a new one) and focus entirely on its API layer as a first-class deliverable: a documented contract other developers could integrate against without asking you questions, a versioning strategy that lets you change the API without breaking existing clients, rate limiting that protects the service, and error responses that are genuinely useful to whoever's calling them. This is a different kind of depth than the Backend capstone -- less about the server's internals, more about the promise you're making to anyone building against your API.
deliverables: Published API documentation (e.g. an OpenAPI/Swagger spec or equivalent) a stranger could use to integrate without reading your source code
A real versioning strategy (URL or header-based), demonstrated with at least one intentional breaking change handled correctly
Rate limiting implemented and documented (limits, and what a client sees when it hits one)
Consistent, correct error semantics across every endpoint -- real status codes, structured error bodies, no 200-with-an-error-inside
A short written note on one client-facing reliability decision you made and why (e.g. pagination strategy, idempotency, timeout/retry guidance for callers)
capstone.portfolioTips: Link the published API docs directly, not just the repo -- a reviewer skimming your portfolio can tell in seconds whether you think about APIs as a product other people depend on, which is a distinct and valuable signal from 'I can build a backend.'

industryUsage.usage: Widely regarded as having some of the best API design and documentation in the industry -- its versioning strategy (explicit API versions per integration) is a commonly cited example of handling breaking changes without breaking existing customers.
Publishes a fully documented, versioned REST and GraphQL API used by a huge ecosystem of third-party tools, with clear rate limiting and error semantics that those tools depend on.
Built its business on API reliability and clarity for external developers -- consistent error responses and predictable rate limits are core to a product where the API IS the product.
